title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 111: Ambergris: Floating Gold of the Oceans
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 111 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Ambergris: Floating Gold of the Oceans

Paragraph 1. For thousands of years, beach walkers along the Atlantic and Indian Oceans sometimes found a strange, strong-smelling lump washed ashore by waves. Known as ambergris, it looked like weathered wax or hard mud. Before scientists understood its origin, ancient cultures invented magical explanations. Arab merchants believed it rose from underwater springs, while Chinese legends claimed it was hardened saliva from sea dragons. Despite its ugly look, ambergris became a priceless trade item for medicine and luxury scents.

Paragraph 2. The true biological source of ambergris was only confirmed in the nineteenth century as commercial whaling expanded. It forms exclusively inside the digestive system of sperm whales, deep-diving hunters that feed mostly on giant squid. While stomach juices easily break down soft squid flesh, hard, sharp squid beaks cannot dissolve. Normally, whales vomit out these beaks; however, occasionally sharp pieces move into the lower intestine and scratch the delicate lining. In response, the whale produces a thick, oily substance to wrap around the sharp beaks, creating a solid mass.

Paragraph 3. Although early scientists assumed this blockage always killed the whale, modern studies show the lump usually passes out naturally into the sea as waste. Fresh raw ambergris is soft, black, and smells strongly of rotting feces. To become valuable, it must float on the ocean for decades. Salt water and direct sunlight slowly bleach and harden it, turning the dark mass into a firm, light grey or white stone with a pleasant, sweet earthy aroma.

Paragraph 4. High-grade cured ambergris often sells for over $20,000 per kilogram thanks to a chemical called ambrein. While ambrein itself has almost no smell, it binds tightly to delicate flower and citrus oils. When used in luxury perfumes, ambrein prevents scents from evaporating quickly on warm skin, allowing fragrances to last for days. Historical records also mention that King Charles II of England enjoyed eating ambergris grated over breakfast eggs.

Paragraph 5. Today, laws governing ambergris vary sharply by country. In the United States, strict wildlife laws forbid owning, buying, or selling any sperm whale product, including lumps found naturally on beaches. Conversely, the United Kingdom and the European Union classify washed-up ambergris as natural ocean waste, making private collection and public auction completely legal. Although chemists have created synthetic substitutes for cheap cosmetics, luxury perfumers insist nothing matches natural ambergris.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...move into the lower intestine and scratch the delicate lining."
Đoạn 3: "...turning the dark mass into a firm, light grey or white stone..."
Đoạn 5: "...classify washed-up ambergris as natural ocean waste..."

q6.text: Scientists confirmed where ambergris came from during the nineteenth century.

steps: Đoạn 2: Nguồn gốc sinh học thật sự được xác nhận vào thế kỷ 19 (nineteenth century).

q7.text: Most sperm whales die quickly when ambergris lumps form inside them.

steps: Đoạn 3: Khối này thường được thải tự nhiên ra biển (passes out naturally), không làm cá chết nhanh.

q8.text: The chemical compound ambrein has practically no smell of its own.

steps: Đoạn 4: "While ambrein itself has almost no smell..."

q9.text: Selling beach-found ambergris is strictly illegal in the United Kingdom.

steps: Đoạn 5: Ở Anh và EU việc nhặt và đấu giá công khai là hoàn toàn hợp pháp (completely legal).

q10.text: White ambergris is much easier to spot on sandy beaches than dark stones.

steps: Đoạn 3 & 5: Bài có nói màu trắng xám của hổ phách lâu năm nhưng không so sánh độ dễ tìm trên bãi cát.
